title: Pitfalls to avoid when going through answers
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton, by his own admission answer-obsessed after observing many lessons, catalogues eleven things teachers commonly say when going through answers or responding to confusion, and explains why each gives weak information or weak help. Reading answers aloud, drawing attention to one question among many visible answers, praising correct answers, aggregating scores and asking for a show of hands all fail to give reliable evidence, or discourage struggling students from speaking up. His fix is to have every student show their actual answer simultaneously on a mini-whiteboard. When misunderstanding appears, he argues that copying corrections, promising to check in later, and asking whether everyone is happy are weak responses, and that explaining and then testing with a similar question is better.
points: Information that is only spoken is transient, so students should be able to read the answers, and revealing them one at a time keeps attention on the question being discussed.
Praising correct answers, tallying scores or asking for raised hands all rely on students admitting confusion in public, so the data is unreliable.
Asking every student to show their answer before discussion is presented as the single most effective way to get honest data on understanding.
Copying down or correcting in coloured pen is described as a myth of copying things down that makes a student feel better without making them understand.
Asking if everyone is happy is a poor proxy for a check, since students stay silent from embarrassment, peer pressure or inability to articulate the problem.
quotes: It is easy for a student to mishear or forget an answer, especially if it is being read out in a big list. Because verbal information is transient, if they miss the answer the first time, there is no opportunity to catch up.

The problem is, if answers to all questions are visible to students, you are fighting a losing battle trying to draw their attention to an earlier question - students are too busy marking and thinking about other answers. Again, there is a simple solution: reveal answers one at a time so you can better control the focus of students’ attention.
Well, put yourself in the shoes of a student who has got the question wrong. Are they really going to put their hand up and say they don’t get it, or ask you to go through it again?

Asking each student to show you their answer to a given question before you have discussed the question or revealed the answer is the single most effective way of obtaining reliable data on student understanding. You hear from all students, and you see their actual answer, not the answer they tell you they got.
Nothing magical happens during the act of copying something from the board into a book which means it all of a sudden makes sense. And yet it looks and feels so much better than a blank answer.

Think of all the reasons a student who does not understand might have for not letting you know: embarrassment, peer pressure, laziness, fear of letting you down, or an inability to articulate exactly what they do not understand. The response to this question is a poor proxy for a reliable whole-class check for understanding.

If students can answer this question correctly - again, mini-whiteboards are your friend here - you have much more reliable evidence that your students are on the path to understanding than a purple-pen adorned book will ever provide.
